article.title: New French Revolution
article.author: Dennis Broe
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The high-school student protest here in France, whose epicenter is the region’s second largest and most diverse city Saint Denis, is every day gathering steam and sometimes forcing the Western corporate media to course correct after their initial slandering of the event. Rather than depicting crowds of students taking to the new barracks—the blockades around their schools— The New York Times initially gleefully ran a video of a burning trash can, as the symbol of this mobilization, implying the demonstrators were violent terrorists. The protests in the high schools, have now spread to universities, and engulf not just the students but also unions, teachers and their parents and grandparents, all come not only to support the protests but also to protect their children and grandchildren from what are the actual terrorists, Macron’s police. The omnipresent banners tell the story about what the students want and what they are reacting to: overcrowding in the schools with teachers who retire or can no longer take the strain not followed by new teachers— “My mother replaces some teachers in burnout but who will replace my mother?”; the call for the state to deal with the problem of underfunding by means other than repressing demonstrators, that is, those who call attention to the problem— “fric non flic,” that is money for education not police; and the unevenness of money spent where those outside Paris and the central cities are more highly underfunded— “Equality does not stop at the gates of the city.” The signs of burning garbage, widespread on American social and corporate media are the mainstream representation of the students’ protest at their future being torn away from them through lack of funding after nine years of Macron’s austerity budgets while also rewarding the richest with major tax breaks. The disparity between the actual protests and how they are being covered also returns to the way the original French Revolution was experienced in the bourgeois media, not as a first attempt at a people’s liberation but as degenerating into what was called “The Terror.” These emblems, emblazoned in young minds in Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities, are regurgitated in today’s bourgeois media where property, even garbage cans, is sacred while the protestor’s are returning to the French writer Proudhoun’s retort, “Property is theft.” Related: The World Cup, the LA Olympics and the Death of Sports Innocence And indeed, the largest protest with leagues of students swarming the square occurred this week at the Bastille, the sight of the beginning of the 1789 Revolution. It was here, at the birthplace of the Revolution, that students acknowledged this heritage by singing “Le Marseillaise,” originally sung on the fly as workers’ militias marched from Marseille to Paris to meld with the Parisian street revolt. Trump has called the protests communist and muslim inspired, claiming these are the twin threats that will bring down America from within, a magnificent and astounding case of projection since the force that is most likely to bring down America from within, the true fifth column, is the Trump family and the Trumpists. Later in the week, with the protests creating an inexorable movement, The Times covered them with a degree of fairness but inserted above their coverage another story about overwhelming French debt hastening an increase in the price of French bonds and making borrowing more difficult for the state. The statement being that there really is no choice other than austerity, no matter what the street may say. On Tuesday afternoon Marine LePen, who leads in the presidential polls to be held next April, unveiled her own proposed budget, a complete sop to the wealthiest corporations, as she proposes to cut approximately $154 billion from the French state. This is as opposed to the other alternative which is frequently advanced and just as quickly dropped of a two percent tax on the wealthiest to maintain France’s social services. Related: Media Watch: The Scandals Behind the Scandals The protesters, since they are still majority high school students, have also called much-needed attention to the Macron government’s standard tactic for dealing with the unrest caused by his government’s transfer of wealth upward, and that is with fierce police violence. A 15-year old’s hand was blown off and 16-year old is now blinded in one eye, most likely struck by an LBD riot gun. Over 5000 mostly high-school students have been arrested and many then held in detention. Students are also upset about another Macron “efficiency innovation” and that is the installation of a Elon Musk-type computer application titled Parcoursup which now handles and supposedly systematizes university applications. The system is slow in getting back to students about whether they have been accepted or rejected while also being accused of favoring those from the wealthiest and best-connected schools. The problem is accentuated by the opaqueness of the system. Nobody knows what criteria it uses in a selection that in France is absolutely crucial in determining the future course of a student’s life. Saint Denis Mayor Bally Bagoyoko protecting students The protests have also been the occasion for accusations against the most popular left party, LFI, claiming that the party and its leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon instigated the rebellion. A popular accusation on the right and center-right, fearful that the second round of the next election could pit the far-right’s Marine Le Pen against LFI’s Mélenchon. The charge has been refuted, even by the centrist Le Monde, no friend of Mélenchon, which claimed in an article on its origins that this was a spontaneous uprising. Where the LFI has been important and where it might make significant gains come next April when many of these students will have reached voting age, is in safeguarding the protestors. A local hero of this revolution is the LFI mayor of Saint Denis Bally Bagoyoko who showed up on the picket lines and put himself in between the police and the demonstrators. Bagayoko is of Malian ancestry and a strong supporter of that country’s, along with Burkina Faso and Niger’s, assertion of its sovereignty in kicking out French troops. He is also a critic of French attempts to recolonize the country, an indication that the revolution on the streets of Paris, its environs and across the country has a global resonance.
